questions.q: Cat detector, starting design $\mathbf{w} = (4, 5, -8)$, $b = -3$. The 🤖 Robo-Dog has $\mathbf{x} = (0.9,\ 0.1,\ 0.8)$. What is $z = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b$, and does the neuron fire (rule: $z \ge 0$)?
questions.explain: $4(0.9) + 5(0.1) - 8(0.8) = 3.6 + 0.5 - 6.4 = -2.3$, then add the bias: $-2.3 - 3 = -5.3 < 0$. $-2.3$ forgets the bias; the negative barking weight is what shuts the Robo-Dog down.

questions.q: With the starting weights the Bunny scores $+8.5$ and the Lion $+8.2$ before the bias. Why can no bias $b$ make the neuron fire for the Lion but not the Bunny?
options: The bias is multiplied by the inputs, so it affects the Bunny more
Any bias below $0$ makes every animal silent
Biases only matter for ReLU, and this neuron uses sigmoid
The bias adds the same number to every animal, so it can only slide the cut-off, never reorder the ranking
questions.explain: Firing for the Lion needs $b \ge -8.2$, which also lets the Bunny ($8.5 + b \ge 0$) through. Only changing the **weights** (e.g. $\mathbf{w} = (0, 10, -8)$, $b = -9.5$) can separate them.

questions.q: Which statement about the neuron's output $y = f(z)$ matches the page?
options: Every activation function outputs a probability between 0 and 1
ReLU outputs are always between 0 and 1
Only sigmoid gives an output in $(0, 1)$, and even that is not a calibrated probability unless trained and checked for it
The step function outputs a calibrated confidence
questions.explain: Sigmoid squashes into $(0, 1)$ and merely *looks* probability-like. ReLU is unbounded above, tanh lies in $(-1, 1)$, and the step function gives a hard 0/1 vote.

questions.q: A layer of 10 neurons reads a 784-dimensional input. How are its weights organized?
options: A $784 \times 10$ matrix with a single shared bias
A $10 \times 784$ matrix (one row per neuron) plus 10 biases
One vector of 784 weights shared by all 10 neurons
questions.explain: Each neuron is one row $\mathbf{w}_i$ of dot products with $\mathbf{x}$, so stacking 10 neurons gives a $10 \times 784$ matrix times the input vector, plus one bias per neuron.
